where 𝒗χ=𝒗−𝒒2​mχ\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}=\boldsymbol{v}-\frac{\boldsymbol{q}}{2m_{\chi}} (with the incoming DM’s velocity 𝒗\boldsymbol{v} and momentum transfer 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} to be integrated over when calculating detection rates), and summation over repeated Cartesian indices is implicit. Here and in what follows, we denote q≡|𝒒|q\equiv|\boldsymbol{q}| (so that q2≡𝒒2≠qμ​qμq^{2}\equiv\boldsymbol{q}^{2}\neq q^{\mu}q_{\mu}), and 𝒒^≡𝒒/q\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\equiv\boldsymbol{q}/q.

To summarize, in the long wavelength limit, the DM-ion scattering potential 𝒱~l​j\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj} involves a set of quantities that characterize properties of the ion: the total numbers ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle}, spins ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle} and orbital angular momenta ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle} of the constituent particles ψ=p,n,e\psi=p,n,e, as well as the spin-orbit coupling tensors ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\bigl\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\bigr\rangle}. We will refer to these as different types of crystal responses, as DM couplings to these quantities drive collective excitations in the crystal; they play a similar role to the nuclear responses in nuclear recoil calculations (which similarly reduce to the total nucleon numbers, spins, etc. in the long wavelength limit [58, 60, 61, 62]). We emphasize, however, that in contrast to standard nuclear recoil where nuclei are treated as free – a valid approximation at energy depositions ≳500\gtrsim 500 meV [33] -- collective excitations arise in a lower energy regime where inter-ionic interactions become important; the EFT therefore involves different degrees of freedom and the calculation proceeds differently.77 7 Technically, Refs. [58, 60] defined a few “nuclear response functions,” WMτ​τ′W_{M}^{\tau\tau^{\prime}}, WΣ′τ​τ′W_{\Sigma^{\prime}}^{\tau\tau^{\prime}} etc., which the nuclear recoil rate is proportional to, from the unpolarized average of nuclear matrix element squared. No such averaging is involved in the calculation of collective excitations, and the rate formulae derived below do not depend on the same functions WMτ​τ′W_{M}^{\tau\tau^{\prime}}, WΣ′τ​τ′W_{\Sigma^{\prime}}^{\tau\tau^{\prime}} etc. even in the absence of coupling to electrons. Here we are simply borrowing the terminology “response” in the sense that it refers to a type of coupling, just as MM, Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, etc., usually called “nuclear responses,” are different types of couplings to the nucleus. We will sometimes abbreviate the crystal responses introduced above as N{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N}, 𝑺{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\boldsymbol{S}}, 𝑳{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\boldsymbol{L}}, 𝑳⊗𝑺{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\boldsymbol{L}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}}, or simply N{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N}, S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S}, L{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L}, L⊗S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L\otimes S}, when there is no confusion. The crystal responses generated by each NR operator and in each benchmark DM model have been summarized in Tables 3 and 2, respectively.

We reiterate that, among the four types of crystal responses, ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle} and ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle} are induced by DM couplings to point-like ionic degrees of freedom (which do not involve internal motions of nucleons or electrons inside an ion), while ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle} and ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\bigl\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\bigr\rangle} are induced by DM couplings to composite degrees of freedom. We therefore refer to them as point-like and composite responses respectively. 𝒗ψ\boldsymbol{v}_{\psi}-independent operators (the first two categories in Table 3) generate point-like responses, while 𝒗ψ\boldsymbol{v}_{\psi}-dependent operators (the last two categories in Table 3) generate composite responses. It is worth noting that operators related by 𝒗χ↔𝒗ψ\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}\leftrightarrow\boldsymbol{v}_{\psi} (e.g. 𝒪3​a\mathcal{O}_{3a} and 𝒪3​b\mathcal{O}_{3b}, 𝒪5​a\mathcal{O}_{5a} and 𝒪5​b\mathcal{O}_{5b}) are usually generated with similar coefficients. For each such pair of operators, the ratio of composite versus point-like responses (i.e. coefficients of ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle} versus ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle}, or ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\bigl\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\bigr\rangle} versus ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle} in Eq. ()) is, parametrically, qmψ​v\frac{q}{m_{\psi}v}. This is generic, as point-like and composite responses result from the leading two terms in the expansion ei​𝒒⋅𝒙α=1+i​𝒒⋅𝒙α+…e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{\alpha}}=1+i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{\alpha}+\dots, and q​x∼qmψ​v​Lqx\sim\frac{q}{m_{\psi}v}L, with L∼𝒪⁡(1)L\sim\mathcal{O}(1). For nuclear recoils (where the two operators have exactly equal and opposite coefficients), qmψ​v∼μχ​Nmp,n\frac{q}{m_{\psi}v}\sim\frac{\mu_{\chi N}}{m_{p,n}} with μχ​N\mu_{\chi N} the reduced mass of the DM and the target nucleus, so composite responses can be significant, as emphasized in Refs. [60, 61]. In contrast, in the present case of collective excitations induced by light DM, we have qmψ​v≲mχmψ\frac{q}{m_{\psi}v}\lesssim\frac{m_{\chi}}{m_{\psi}}. For couplings to nucleons, ψ=p,n\psi=p,n, this ratio is always smaller than one for sub-GeV DM, so for a given type of excitation, point-like responses tend to dominate; for couplings to electrons, ψ=e\psi=e, both point-like and composite responses, if present, can be important. From the bottom-up point of view, it is useful to keep in mind this interplay between point-like and composite responses for the purpose of organizing the effects of various operators, although from the top-down point of view, it seems difficult to construct well-motivated simple models that dominantly generate a composite response (L{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L} or L⊗S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L\otimes S}) without being accompanied by a point-like response (N{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N} or S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S}) of at least comparable size, similar to the case of nuclear recoil as highlighted in Ref. [61]. We will elaborate on this in Sec. III.

II.3 Quantization of Lattice Potential for Phonons and Magnons

Now that we have obtained 𝒱~l​j\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj} in terms of the lattice degrees of freedom, Eq. (), it remains to compute the matrix elements

⟨ν,𝒌​|𝒱~​(−𝒒,𝒗)|​0⟩=∑l,j⟨ν,𝒌​|ei​𝒒⋅𝒙l​j​𝒱~l​j​(−𝒒,𝒗)|​0⟩\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\,\widetilde{\cal V}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})|0\rangle=\sum_{l,j}\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}}\,\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})|0\rangle (28)

by quantizing the lattice potential in terms of phonon or magnon modes. The simplest cases, where phonon excitations in a crystal proceed through ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle} (via the SI operator 𝒪1=𝟙\mathcal{O}_{1}=\mathbb{1}) and magnon excitations proceed through ⟨𝑺e⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle} were considered previously in Refs. [53, 54, 33, 34] and Ref. [57], respectively. Here we extend those calculations to include all four crystal responses (⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle}, ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}, ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle}, ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}) identified in the previous subsection, which can be generated by the full set of effective operators.

Phonons arise from the ions’ displacements with respect to their equilibrium positions 𝒙l​j0\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}:

𝒖l​j=𝒙l​j−𝒙l​j0=∑ν=13​n∑𝒌∈1BZ12​N​mj​ων,𝒌(a^ν,𝒌ϵν,𝒌,jei​𝒌⋅𝒙l​j0+a^ν,𝒌†ϵν,𝒌,j∗e−i𝒌⋅𝒙l​j0).\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}=\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}-\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}=\sum_{\nu=1}^{3n}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\text{1BZ}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2Nm_{j}\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}}\Bigl(\,\hat{a}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}}+\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}\,e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}}\Bigr)\,. (29)

Recall that NN (without subscript, not to be confused with ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle}) is the total number of primitive cells in the crystal lattice, to be sent to infinity at the end of the calculation. The phonon creation and annihilation operators satisfy the canonical commutation relations, [a^ν,𝒌,a^ν′,𝒌′†]=δν​ν′​δ𝒌,𝒌′[\hat{a}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}},\hat{a}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}]=\delta_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}\delta_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}} with all others vanishing. The eigenenergies ων,𝒌\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}} and eigenvectors ϵν,𝒌,j\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j} (normalized such that ∑j|ϵν,𝒌,j|2=1\sum_{j}|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}|^{2}=1) are solved for by diagonalizing the quadratic crystal potential. The quadratic crystal potential, and equilibrium positions, are computed with DFT [78] (see Refs. [54, 34] for details) and the diagonalization is performed with phonopy [65]. At leading order, dependence of the matrix element in Eq. (28) on 𝒖l​j\boldsymbol{u}_{lj} comes only from the phase factor ei​𝒒⋅𝒙l​je^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}}; we assume the DM-ion scattering potentials 𝒱~l​j​(−𝒒,𝒗)\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v}) are not significantly affected by ionic displacements and can thus be pulled out of the matrix element.88 8 If 𝒱~l​j\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj} receives contributions from DM-electron couplings, the scattering potential can depend on 𝒖l​j\boldsymbol{u}_{lj} directly, as ionic displacements distort the electron wavefunctions. This correction can be taken into account via the Born effective charges in the case of SI interactions in the long wavelength limit, as discussed in Ref. [33]. Then, evaluating the matrix element of the phase factor, ⟨ν,𝒌​|ei​𝒒⋅𝒙l​j|​0⟩\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}}|0\rangle, follows the standard procedure of expanding 𝒙l​j\boldsymbol{x}_{lj} as in Eq. (29) and applying the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula to normal-order the phonon creation and annihilation operators [33]. As a result,

⟨ν,𝒌​|𝒱~​(−𝒒,𝒗)|​0⟩=1N​∑ν,𝒌,j[∑l𝒱~l​j​(−𝒒,𝒗)​ei⁡(𝒒−𝒌)⋅𝒙l​j0]​e−Wj​(𝒒)​i⁡(𝒒⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗)2​mj​ων,𝒌,\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\,\widetilde{\cal V}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})|0\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}\Biggl[\sum_{l}\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\,e^{i(\boldsymbol{q}-\boldsymbol{k})\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}}\Biggr]e^{-W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})}\,\frac{i(\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{*}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j})}{\sqrt{2m_{j}\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}}\,, (30)

where Wj​(𝒒)=14​N​mj​∑ν,𝒌|𝒒⋅ϵν,𝒌,j|2ων,𝒌W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})=\frac{1}{4Nm_{j}}\sum_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\frac{|\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}|^{2}}{\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}} is the Debye-Waller factor. Crucially, the 1N\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} factor (which originates from Eq. (29) and is to be squared when computing the rate), together with the prefactor 1V\frac{1}{V} in the rate formula Eq. (5), indicates that the rate Γ\Gamma would scale as 1N2→0\frac{1}{N^{2}}\to 0 unless the ll sum in Eq. (30) scales with NN. This in turn requires the NN terms in the ll sum to add up coherently, which is possible only when i) the phonon momentum 𝒌\boldsymbol{k} matches the momentum transfer 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} up to reciprocal lattice vectors, which is the statement of lattice momentum conservation, and ii) ∑l𝒱~l​j∼N\sum_{l}\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj}\sim N, i.e. the DM couples coherently across the crystal lattice. The second requirement is trivially satisfied for DM couplings to the scalar quantities ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle}, tr​(⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩)\text{tr}({\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}). For couplings to the vector and tensor quantities ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}, ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle}, ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle} (modulo the trace part), on the other hand, coherence is possible only when they are ordered (or polarized), so that they point in the same directions in all primitive cells; in the case of ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}, this can be achieved by spontaneous magnetic ordering for ψ=e\psi=e, or by applying an external magnetic field for ψ=p,n\psi=p,n.

Up to possible small corrections due to the presence of different isotopes, we can set 𝒱~l​j=𝒱~j\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj}=\widetilde{\cal V}_{j}, which is independent of ll. We then obtain the single phonon excitation rate:

Γ⁡(𝒗)=1Ω​∫d3​q(2​π)3​∑ν=13​n 2​π​δ​(ων,𝒌−ω𝒒)​12​ων,𝒌​|∑je−Wj​(𝒒)​ei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​𝒒⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗mj​𝒱~j​(−𝒒,𝒗)|2,\Gamma(\boldsymbol{v})=\frac{1}{\Omega}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\nu=1}^{3n}\,2\pi\,\delta\bigl(\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}-\omega_{\boldsymbol{q}}\bigr)\frac{1}{2\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}\biggl|\sum_{j}e^{-W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})}e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\,\frac{\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}\,\widetilde{\cal V}_{j}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\biggr|^{2}\,, (31)

where Ω\Omega is the volume of the primitive cell, 𝒙j0\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0} is the equilibrium position of the jjth ion with respect to the cell center, and it is implicit that 𝒒=𝒌+𝑮\boldsymbol{q}=\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G} where 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} is a reciprocal lattice vector. To map 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} to a vector 𝒌\boldsymbol{k} within the 1BZ, we first write 𝒒=∑i=13ai​𝒃i\boldsymbol{q}=\sum_{i=1}^{3}a_{i}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}, with 𝒃i\boldsymbol{b}_{i} the basis vectors of the reciprocal lattice, then construct a set of eight candidate 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} vectors whose components in reduced coordinates take the floor and ceiling integer values of aia_{i}, and finally choose the correct 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} vector to be the one that minimizes |𝒒−𝑮||\boldsymbol{q}-\boldsymbol{G}|.

The DM-ion scattering potential 𝒱~j\widetilde{\cal V}_{j} that enters Eq. (31) is simply given by Eq. () above, with the ll subscripts dropped, assuming ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}, ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle}, ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle} are ordered, as explained above; in the absence of ordering, the corresponding terms should be dropped (with ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle} set to its scalar component 13​tr​(⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩)​𝟙=13​⟨𝑳ψ⋅𝑺ψ⟩​𝟙\frac{1}{3}\,\text{tr}({\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle})\,\mathbb{1}=\frac{1}{3}\,\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle\,\mathbb{1}). In the special case of SI interactions, one has only c1(ψ)c_{1}^{(\psi)}, so V~j=∑ψc1(ψ)​⟨Nψ⟩j\widetilde{V}_{j}=\sum_{\psi}c_{1}^{(\psi)}{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle}_{j}, reproducing the results in Ref. [33], whereas in the full EFT, all four crystal responses can contribute to phonon excitations.

Next we move on to magnons. They are collective spin excitations in a magnetically ordered phase, and can thus respond to DM scattering only if the potentials 𝒱~l​j\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj} depend on the magnetic ions’ effective spins 𝑺l​j\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}. Generally, 𝑺l​j\boldsymbol{S}_{lj} can come from the electrons’ spin and orbital angular momenta, ⟨𝑺e⟩l​j{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle}_{lj} and ⟨𝑳e⟩l​j{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{e}\rangle}_{lj}, respectively. When projected onto the Hilbert space spanned by 𝑺l​j\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}, they become

⟨𝑺e⟩l​j→λS,j​𝑺l​j,⟨𝑳e⟩l​j→λL,j​𝑺l​j,{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle}_{lj}\to\lambda_{S,j}\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}\,,\qquad{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{e}\rangle}_{lj}\to\lambda_{L,j}\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}\,, (32)

where λS,j\lambda_{S,j}, λL,j\lambda_{L,j} are numbers (which we will say more about shortly). Therefore, from Eq. () we obtain the matrix element for exciting a magnon mode |ν,𝒌⟩|\nu,\boldsymbol{k}\rangle:

⟨ν,𝒌​|𝒱~​(−𝒒,𝒗)|​0⟩=∑l,jei​𝒒⋅𝒙l​j​𝒇j​(−𝒒,𝒗)⋅⟨ν,𝒌​|𝑺l​j|​0⟩,\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\,\widetilde{\cal V}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})|0\rangle=\sum_{l,j}e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}}\boldsymbol{f}_{j}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\cdot\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}|0\rangle\,, (33)

where

𝒇j​(−𝒒,𝒗)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}_{j}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v}) =\displaystyle= λS,j[c3​a(e)i​qme(𝒒^×𝒗χ)+c4(e)𝑺χ+c6(e)q2me2(𝒒^⋅𝑺χ)𝒒^+c7​a(e)𝒗χ+c9(e)i​qme(𝒒^×𝑺χ)+c10(e)i​𝒒me\displaystyle\lambda_{S,j}\biggl[c_{3a}^{(e)}\frac{iq}{m_{e}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\times\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}\bigr)+c_{4}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}+c_{6}^{(e)}\frac{q^{2}}{m_{e}^{2}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\bigr)\,\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}+c_{7a}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}+c_{9}^{(e)}\frac{iq}{m_{e}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\times\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\bigr)+c_{10}^{(e)}\frac{i\boldsymbol{q}}{m_{e}} (34)
+c12​a(e)(𝒗χ×𝑺χ)+c13​a(e)i​𝒒me(𝒗χ⋅𝑺χ)+c14​a(e)i​qme(𝒒^⋅𝑺χ)𝒗χ−c15​a(e)q2me2(𝒒^⋅(𝒗χ×𝑺χ))𝒒^]\displaystyle\;\;+c_{12a}^{(e)}\bigl(\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}\times\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\bigr)+c_{13a}^{(e)}\frac{i\boldsymbol{q}}{m_{e}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\bigr)+c_{14a}^{(e)}\frac{iq}{m_{e}}\left(\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\right)\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}-c_{15a}^{(e)}\frac{q^{2}}{m_{e}^{2}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\cdot(\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}\times\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi})\bigr)\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\biggr]
+λL,j2[−c5​b(e)q2me2(𝟙−𝒒^𝒒^)⋅𝑺χ+c8​b(e)i​qme(𝒒^×𝑺χ)].\displaystyle+\frac{\lambda_{L,j}}{2}\biggl[-c_{5b}^{(e)}\frac{q^{2}}{m_{e}^{2}}\bigl(\mathbb{1}-\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\bigr)\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}+c_{8b}^{(e)}\frac{iq}{m_{e}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\times\boldsymbol{S}_{\chi}\bigr)\biggr]\,.

As in Eq. (), we have defined q≡|𝒒|q\equiv|\boldsymbol{q}|, 𝒒^≡𝒒/q\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\equiv\boldsymbol{q}/q, and 𝒗χ=𝒗−𝒒2​mχ\boldsymbol{v}_{\chi}=\boldsymbol{v}-\frac{\boldsymbol{q}}{2m_{\chi}}.

Now we need to compute ⟨ν,𝒌​|𝑺l​j|​0⟩\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}|0\rangle. The calculation follows Ref. [57], which we encourage the reader to consult for more details. The magnetic order is captured by a set of rotation matrices 𝐑j{\bf R}_{j} that take each 𝑺l​j\boldsymbol{S}_{lj} to a local coordinate system where it points in the +z+z direction:

𝑺l​j=𝐑j⋅𝑺l​j′,⟨𝑺l​j′⟩=(⟨Sl​j′x⟩,⟨Sl​j′y⟩,⟨Sl​j′z⟩)=(0, 0,Sj).\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}={\bf R}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}^{\prime}_{lj}\,,\qquad\quad\langle\boldsymbol{S}^{\prime}_{lj}\rangle=\bigl(\langle S^{\prime x}_{lj}\rangle,\,\langle S^{\prime y}_{lj}\rangle,\,\langle S^{\prime z}_{lj}\rangle\bigr)=\bigl(0,\,0,\,S_{j}\bigr)\,. (35)

We restrict ourselves to commensurate orders, in which case the rotation matrices 𝐑j{\bf R}_{j} do not depend on the primitive cell label ll. We then apply the Holstein-Primakoff transformation and expand 𝑺l​j\boldsymbol{S}_{lj} around the ground state in terms of bosonic creation and annihilation operators:

Sl​j′x=(2​Sj−a^l​j†​a^l​j)1/2​a^l​j,Sl​j′y=a^l​j†​(2​Sj−a^l​j†​a^l​j)1/2,Sl​j′z=Sj−a^l​j†​a^l​j.S^{\prime x}_{lj}=\bigl(2S_{j}-\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{lj}\hat{a}_{lj}\bigr)^{1/2}\,\hat{a}_{lj}\,,\qquad S^{\prime y}_{lj}=\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{lj}\,\bigl(2S_{j}-\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{lj}\hat{a}_{lj}\bigr)^{1/2}\,,\qquad S^{\prime z}_{lj}=S_{j}-\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{lj}\hat{a}_{lj}\,. (36)

Magnon eigenstates are obtained by diagonalizing the spin Hamiltonian, which is specific to the target material; in the simplest cases, the target can be modeled by Heisenberg exchange interactions 𝑺l​j⋅𝑺l′​j′\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{l^{\prime}j^{\prime}} between neighboring sites, while more complicated model descriptions are needed in other cases. For a general spin Hamiltonian, the diagonalization can be achieved by a Bogoliubov transformation in momentum space:

a^l​j=1N​∑𝒌∈1BZa^j,𝒌​ei​𝒌⋅𝒙l​j,(a^j,𝒌a^j,−𝒌†)=(𝕌j​ν,𝒌𝕍j​ν,𝒌𝕍j​ν,−𝒌∗𝕌j​ν,−𝒌∗)​(b^j,𝒌b^j,−𝒌†),\hat{a}_{lj}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\text{1BZ}}\hat{a}_{j,\boldsymbol{k}}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}}\,,\qquad\left(\begin{matrix}\hat{a}_{j,\boldsymbol{k}}\\ \hat{a}_{j,-\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}\end{matrix}\right)=\left(\begin{matrix}\mathbb{U}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}&\mathbb{V}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\\ \mathbb{V}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}^{*}&\mathbb{U}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}^{*}\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}\hat{b}_{j,\boldsymbol{k}}\\ \hat{b}_{j,-\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}\end{matrix}\right)\,, (37)

where 𝕌\mathbb{U}, 𝕍\mathbb{V} are n×nn\times n matrices (with nn the number of magnetic ions per cell), and b^j,𝒌†\hat{b}_{j,\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}, b^j,𝒌\hat{b}_{j,\boldsymbol{k}} are the creation and annihilation operators for the magnon eigenstates satisfying canonical commutation relations, [b^ν,𝒌,b^ν′,𝒌′†]=δν​ν′​δ𝒌,𝒌′[\hat{b}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}},\hat{b}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}]=\delta_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}\delta_{\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}} with all others vanishing. An efficient algorithm for the diagonalization can be found in Ref. [66] (see also Refs. [57, 79]). Now computing the magnon excitation matrix element ⟨ν,𝒌​|𝑺l​j|​0⟩\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|\boldsymbol{S}_{lj}|0\rangle, and hence the DM scattering rate, is reduced to standard algebra. We obtain [57, 79]

Γ⁡(𝒗)=1Ω​∫d3​q(2​π)3​∑ν=1n 2​π​δ​(ων,𝒌−ω𝒒)​12​|∑jei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​Sj​(𝕌j​ν,𝒌∗​𝒓j+𝕍j​ν,−𝒌​𝒓j∗)⋅𝒇j​(−𝒒,𝒗)|2,\Gamma(\boldsymbol{v})=\frac{1}{\Omega}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\nu=1}^{n}\,2\pi\,\delta\bigl(\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}-\omega_{\boldsymbol{q}}\bigr)\,\frac{1}{2}\,\biggl|\sum_{j}e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\sqrt{S_{j}}\,\bigl(\mathbb{U}^{*}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}+\mathbb{V}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{*}\bigr)\cdot\boldsymbol{f}_{j}(-\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{v})\biggr|^{2}\,, (38)

where 𝒓j=(Rjx​x,Rjy​x,Rjz​x)+i⁡(Rjx​y,Rjy​y,Rjz​y)\boldsymbol{r}_{j}=(R_{j}^{xx},\,R_{j}^{yx},\,R_{j}^{zx})+i\,(R_{j}^{xy},\,R_{j}^{yy},\,R_{j}^{zy}). As in the phonon case, it is implicit that 𝒌\boldsymbol{k} matches 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} up to a reciprocal lattice vector, 𝒒=𝒌+𝑮\boldsymbol{q}=\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G}, due to lattice momentum conservation.

A comment is in order about the target choice. In the case where the total 𝑺l​j\boldsymbol{S}_{lj} involve only spin degrees of freedom (as is the case for yttrium iron garnet (YIG) discussed in Ref. [57]), λS,j=1\lambda_{S,j}=1, λL,j=0\lambda_{L,j}=0, and only the first two lines of Eq. (34) are relevant. Targets for which λL,j≠0\lambda_{L,j}\neq 0 are more exotic. One class of materials with λL,j≠0\lambda_{L,j}\neq 0 is spin-orbit-entangled Mott insulators [80, 81, 82], where the combined effect of crystal fields and spin-orbit coupling results in effective spins Sj=12S_{j}=\frac{1}{2}, and we can show that λS,j=−13\lambda_{S,j}=-\frac{1}{3}, λL,j=−43\lambda_{L,j}=-\frac{4}{3} (see Appendix B for details, and Refs. [83, 81, 82, 84] for related discussion), so the magnetic ions’ effective spins are in fact dominated by their orbital components. Perovskite irridates such as Sr2IrO4 [83, 80] and Kitaev materials Na2IrO3, α\alpha-RuCl3 [85, 82, 86, 84] are among the materials with this feature that have been actively studied recently by the condensed matter physics community. While perhaps futuristic as DM detectors, such materials have the novel feature of being sensitive to DM couplings with electrons’ orbital angular momenta.

As a final remark, we note from the derivation above that when the same crystal response, ⟨𝑺e⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle} or ⟨𝑳e⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{e}\rangle}, excites both phonons and magnons, the phonon excitation rate is parametrically suppressed by q2mion​ω∼10−2​(qkeV)2​(10​GeVmion)​(10​meVω)\frac{q^{2}}{m_{\text{ion}}\omega}\sim 10^{-2}\bigl(\frac{q}{\text{keV}}\bigr)^{2}\bigl(\frac{10\,\text{GeV}}{m_{\text{ion}}}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{10\,\text{meV}}{\omega}\bigr). Thus, for example, for the second group of operators in Table 3 with ψ=e\psi=e, which generates ⟨𝑺e⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle} response, single magnon excitation is expected to achieve better sensitivity than single phonon excitation for the same exposure and detector efficiency. On the other hand, since phonons can be excited also by other crystal responses, they have a broader coverage of the DM theory space. We will investigate the interplay between single phonon and magnon excitations in the context of our benchmark models in the next section.

III Application to Benchmark Models

We now apply the general results of the previous section to the set of benchmark models in Table 2. The first step of the calculation – matching the relativistic model onto the NR EFT – was already done in Sec. II.1. The results are the operator coefficients ci(ψ)c_{i}^{(\psi)} listed in the second to last column of Table 2. We then need to substitute these operator coefficients into the formulae derived in Secs. II.2 and II.3 to compute direct detection rates Γ⁡(𝒗)\Gamma(\boldsymbol{v}) — Eq. (31) together with Eq. () for single phonon excitations, and Eq. (38) together with Eq. (34) for single magnon excitations.

In order to present the results in a concise way, let us introduce the following definitions. For single phonon excitation, we define (cf. Eq. (31))

FX,ν(ψ)​(𝒒)≡∑je−Wj​(𝒒)​ei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​𝒒⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗2​mj​ων,𝒌​⟨Xψ⟩j,F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)}(\boldsymbol{q})\equiv\sum_{j}e^{-W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})}e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\,\frac{\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}}{\sqrt{2m_{j}\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle X_{\psi}\rangle}_{j}\,, (39)

where XX represents one of the crystal responses, X=N,S,L,L⊗SX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L\otimes S}; note that FX,ν(ψ)F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} are vector (tensor) quantities when X=S,LX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L} (X=L⊗SX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L\otimes S}), and will be written as 𝑭X,ν(ψ)\boldsymbol{F}_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} (𝐅X,ν(ψ){\bf F}_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)}). These FX,ν(ψ)F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} play the role of form factors for exciting a single phonon via a certain type of response. For single magnon excitation, we define (cf. Eq. (38))

𝑬X,ν​(𝒒)≡∑jei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​Sj2​(𝕌j​ν,𝒌∗​𝒓j+𝕍j​ν,−𝒌​𝒓j∗)​λX,j,\boldsymbol{E}_{X,\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})\equiv\sum_{j}e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\,\sqrt{\frac{S_{j}}{2}}\,\bigl(\mathbb{U}^{*}_{j\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}+\mathbb{V}_{j\nu,-\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{r}_{j}^{*}\bigr)\,\lambda_{X,j}\,, (40)

where X=S,LX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L}. These are formally analogous to polarization vectors of a vector field. In both Eqs. (39) and (40), 𝒌\boldsymbol{k} is the phonon momentum inside the 1BZ that satisfies 𝒒=𝒌+𝑮\boldsymbol{q}=\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G} for some reciprocal lattice vector 𝑮\boldsymbol{G}; as emphasized below Eq. (31), 𝒌\boldsymbol{k} is uniquely determined by mapping 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} into the 1BZ through reciprocal lattice vectors. We further define a set of quantities Σν​(𝒒)\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q}), for both single phonon and single magnon excitations, by (cf. Eq. (5))

Γ⁡(𝒗)≡1Ω​∫d3​q(2​π)3​∑ν 2​π​δ​(ων,𝒌−ω𝒒)​Σν​(𝒒).\Gamma(\boldsymbol{v})\equiv\frac{1}{\Omega}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\nu}\,2\pi\,\delta\bigl(\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}-\omega_{\boldsymbol{q}}\bigr)\,\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})\,. (41)

We will refer to Σν​(𝒒)\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q}), which have mass dimension −4-4, as “differential rates.” Practically, Σν​(𝒒)\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q}) are obtained simply by taking 𝒱~l​j\widetilde{\cal V}_{lj} in Eq. (), substituting ⟨Xψ⟩l​j{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle X_{\psi}\rangle}_{lj} by FX,ν(ψ)F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} (for ψ=p,n,e\psi=p,n,e and X=N,S,L,L⊗SX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L\otimes S}) or 𝑬X,ν\boldsymbol{E}_{X,\nu} (for ψ=e\psi=e only, and X=S,LX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L}), squaring it and averaging over the DM’s spin (which amounts to replacing Sχi​Sχk→14​δi​kS_{\chi}^{i}S_{\chi}^{k}\to\frac{1}{4}\delta^{ik}). As we will see, written in terms of the dimensionless quantities FX,ν(ψ)F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} and 𝑬X,ν\boldsymbol{E}_{X,\nu} defined above, Σν​(𝒒)\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q}) can be expressed in a concise form for each benchmark model. This will be convenient when we compare the rates between different models, and between phonon and magnon excitations.

Our final results will be presented in terms of the rate per unit target mass,

R=1ρT​ρχmχ​∫d3​v​fχ​(𝒗)​Γ​(𝒗),R=\frac{1}{\rho_{T}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\int d^{3}v\,f_{\chi}(\boldsymbol{v})\,\Gamma(\boldsymbol{v})\,, (42)

where ρT\rho_{T} is the target’s mass density that we take from Ref. [87], ρχ=0.4​GeV/cm3\rho_{\chi}=0.4\,\text{GeV}/\text{cm}^{3} is the local DM mass density, and fχ​(𝒗)f_{\chi}(\boldsymbol{v}) is the DM’s velocity distribution, taken to be a boosted and truncated Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution — see Appendix C for technical details of evaluating the velocity integrals. For the projected reach, we assume 3 events per kilogram-year exposure, corresponding to 95% C.L. exclusion in a background-free counting experiment, and assume a detector energy threshold of 1 meV. While we will present full numerical results, the main features can usually be understood by simple parametric estimates. Generally, noting that the velocity integral over the energy conserving delta function δ⁡(ων,𝒌−ω𝒒)\delta(\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}-\omega_{\boldsymbol{q}}) yields a function that scales as q−1q^{-1} (see Appendix C), we have from Eqs. (41) and (42), parametrically,

R∼ρχmχ​1mcell​∫d​q​q​Σ,R\sim\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\int dq\,q\,\Sigma\,, (43)

where mcell=ρT​Ωm_{\text{cell}}=\rho_{T}\Omega is the mass of the primitive cell, and as before, q=|𝒒|q=|\boldsymbol{q}|. Then, from the formulas for Σν​(𝒒)\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q}) presented below for each model in terms of FX,ν(ψ)F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} and 𝑬X,ν\boldsymbol{E}_{X,\nu} defined in Eqs. (39) and (40), we can estimate the rate RR by

FX,ν(ψ)∼qmion​ω​⟨Xψ⟩,𝑬X,ν∼Sion.F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)}\sim\frac{q}{\sqrt{m_{\text{ion}}\omega}}\langle X_{\psi}\rangle\,,\qquad\boldsymbol{E}_{X,\nu}\sim\sqrt{S_{\text{ion}}}\,. (44)

In the case of single phonon excitations, we should further note that ω\omega, which appears in FX,ν(ψ)F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} above, can scale differently with qq for different models and DM masses. Typically, either acoustic phonons (associated with in-phase oscillations) or optical phonons (associated with out-of-phase oscillations) dominate the total rate, depending on whether the DM model couples to different ions in a correlated or anti-correlated way. For acoustic phonons, and for qq within the 1BZ, ω∼cs​q\omega\sim c_{s}q (with csc_{s} the sound speed that is typically 𝒪⁡(10−5)\mathcal{O}(10^{-5})), whereas for optical phonons or for qq beyond the 1BZ, ω∼q0\omega\sim q^{0}. The size of the 1BZ is set by the inverse lattice spacing a−1a^{-1}, and is typically 𝒪⁡(keV)\mathcal{O}(\text{keV}). Since v∼𝒪⁡(10−3)v\sim\mathcal{O}(10^{-3}), contributions from outside the 1BZ are possible for DM masses above around an MeV. We will see below that in several cases, the curves scale differently for mχ≲m_{\chi}\lesssim MeV and mχ≳m_{\chi}\gtrsim MeV for this reason.

On the target side, we will consider the following representative set of materials:

  • •

    GaAs [phonons, subject of R&D]. As the first-studied target for DM detection via phonons, GaAs is already in R&D as a target for both electron excitations and phonon excitations [88]. Phonons in GaAs form 3 acoustic and 3 optical branches, and have energies up to ∼\sim35 meV.

  • •

    SiO2 (quartz) [phonons, optimal sensitivity]. Based on our previous theoretical study comparing the phonon reach of a variety of target materials [34], we have advocated quartz as having good sensitivity to DM couplings to both acoustic and optical phonons. Also, quartz has complementary features compared to GaAs: while GaAs has a simple crystal structure and relatively low phonon energies, quartz has a large number of phonon branches (3 acoustic, 24 optical), with energies up to ∼150\sim 150 meV.

  • •

    Y3Fe5O12 (YIG) [mostly magnons, also phonons for comparison]. YIG is a well studied material with ferrimagnetic order, and is already used in an axion DM detection experiment QUAX [89, 90, 91, 92, 93]. The effective spin Hamiltonian is a Heisenberg model, with Sj=52S_{j}=\frac{5}{2} for the magnetic Fe3+ ions coming entirely from electron spins ⟨𝑺e⟩\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle (i.e. λS,j=1\lambda_{S,j}=1, λL,j=0\lambda_{L,j}=0 in Eq. (40)). We take the antiferromagnetic exchange coupling parameters from Ref. [94], together with the crystal parameters from Ref. [87], to compute the magnon spectrum and rotation matrices. YIG has 20 magnon branches, one of which is gapless and has a quadratic dispersion at small kk. The gapped magnons have energies up to ∼90\sim 90 meV. We will mostly consider YIG as a candidate material for DM detection via magnon excitations, but will also consider phonon excitations in YIG via DM couplings to the ordered electron spins in Sec. III.1 for comparison; in this case the scattering potential is determined by ⟨𝑺e⟩l​j{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle}_{lj} of the Fe3+ ions, which have magnitude 52\frac{5}{2} and directions set by the ferrimagnetic order. YIG has 80 ions in total in the primitive cell and therefore 240 phonon branches (3 acoustic, 237 optical), with energies up to ∼120\sim 120 meV.

  • •

    α\alpha-RuCl3 [small-gap magnons with orbital component]. As discussed below Eq. (34), α\alpha-RuCl3 is one of the materials where the effective ionic spins involve orbital degrees of freedom, and is therefore sensitive to DM couplings to the electrons’ orbital angular momenta. The magnetic ions Ru3+ have Sl​j=12S_{lj}=\frac{1}{2}, coming from both ⟨𝑺e⟩\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle and ⟨𝑳e⟩\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{e}\rangle with λS,j=−13\lambda_{S,j}=-\frac{1}{3}, λL,j=−43\lambda_{L,j}=-\frac{4}{3}, as discussed in Appendix B. The effective spin Hamiltonian features Kitaev-type bond-directional exchange couplings. We use the Hamiltonian parameters derived from neutron scattering data in Ref. [95], which also includes an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange; see Ref. [86] for a summary of some alternative model parameterizations derived from a variety of experimental and numerical techniques. The resulting magnetic order is zig-zag antiferromagnetic. Magnons in α\alpha-RuCl3, of which there are 4 branches, are at very low energy, below 7 meV, and can thus probe lighter DM than YIG. Also, since all magnon branches are gapped at zero momentum, the sensitivity is not significantly affected by the finite detector threshold. This is in contrast with YIG, where the assumed 1 meV energy threshold limits the momentum transfer to be greater than ∼80\sim 80 eV in order to excite magnons on the gapless branch. Therefore, even though the experimental prospects of α\alpha-RuCl3 itself are unclear, it can be regarded as a useful benchmark which highlights the generic advantage of small-gap targets.

Our main results are Figs. 1-4. We give a brief summary here and discuss them in more detail in the following subsections. A major issue of interest is the comparison of sensitivity to various types of DM interactions, via single phonon and magnon excitations induced by various crystal responses. First, we consider the standard SD interaction in Fig. 1, where we see that magnons outperform phonons, typically, by more than an order of magnitude in terms of the coupling reach. Next, in Fig. 2, we compare the phonon and magnon rates for the four combinations of scalar mediator couplings; the phonon production rate is larger, if the scalar and pseudoscalar couplings are of the same order, while magnons allow access to the models where the mediator dominantly couples to the pseudoscalar currents of SM fermions. Next, we compare the reach of phonons and magnons to multipole models in Fig. 3; for the magnetic dipole and anapole models we expect the magnon reach to be better, and indeed it is. However, the phonon reach from quartz is sufficiently strong that, given the greater experimental challenges currently associated with magnon read-out, quartz should be considered a competitor for these models. Lastly, in Fig. 4, we compare theoretical reach in the (𝑳⋅𝑺)(\boldsymbol{L}\cdot\boldsymbol{S})-interacting model, where magnons outperform phonons for sub-MeV DM with the same exposure; however, the (𝑳⋅𝑺)(\boldsymbol{L}\cdot\boldsymbol{S})-interacting model is difficult to UV complete, and our calculation is perhaps somewhat an academic exercise that demonstrate aspects of the EFT.

We now discuss each benchmark model in turn.

III.1 Standard Spin-Dependent Interaction

For the standard SD interaction there is only one operator, 𝒪4\mathcal{O}_{4}, which generates the S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S} response, and can excite both phonons and magnons in a magnetically ordered target. Here, only couplings to electrons (whose spins are ordered) are relevant, and we obtain, for the differential rates,

Σν​(𝒒)phonon\displaystyle\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})_{\text{phonon}} =\displaystyle= 4​gχ2​ge2mV4​|𝑭S,ν(e)|2,\displaystyle\frac{4g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}}\,\bigl|\boldsymbol{F}_{S,\nu}^{(e)}\bigr|^{2}\,, (45)
Σν​(𝒒)magnon\displaystyle\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})_{\text{magnon}} =\displaystyle= 4​gχ2​ge2mV4​|𝑬S,ν|2.\displaystyle\frac{4g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}}\,\bigl|\boldsymbol{E}_{S,\nu}\bigr|^{2}\,. (46)

In Fig. 1, we compare the phonon and magnon reach with YIG. As a technical note, in the absence of a DFT calculation for the crystal potential in YIG which is necessary for computing the phonon eigenmodes, we estimate the rate in two ways. First, we carry out an approximate analytic calculation taking into account long-wavelength acoustic phonons, as explained in Appendix D. This results in the dashed reach curve in Fig. 1, which is truncated at the DM mass for which the maximum momentum transfer reaches the edge of the 1BZ, so that the approximations we make cease to hold. Second, we borrow the crystal potential of Y3Ga5O12 (YGG) which is publicly available [96]. YGG has the same crystal structure as YIG, with Fe replaced by Ga, and the phonon dispersions we obtain for YGG are very similar to those of YIG [97]. The resulting reach is shown by the solid blue curve in Fig. 1. We see from the figure that both estimates are in good agreement near mχ∼10−2m_{\chi}\sim 10^{-2} MeV, where acoustic phonons dominate, while including optical phonon contributions in the second approach improves the reach at lower and higher mχm_{\chi}.

We can understand these curves by estimating the rates using Eqs. (43) and (44). The qq integrals are dominated by qmax∼mχ​vq_{\text{max}}\sim m_{\chi}v. As a result,

Rphonon\displaystyle R_{\text{phonon}} ∼\displaystyle\sim ρχmχ​1mcell​gχ2​ge2mV4​Sion2mion​∫d​q​q3ω\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}^{2}}{m_{\text{ion}}}\int dq\,\frac{q^{3}}{\omega} (47)
∼\displaystyle\sim {gχ2​ge2mV4​ρχmχ​Sion2mcell​mion​cs​(mχ​v)3(acoustic, mχ​v≲a−1),gχ2​ge2mV4​ρχmχ​Sion2mcell​mion​⟨ω⟩​(mχ​v)4(otherwise),\displaystyle\begin{cases}\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}^{2}}{m_{\text{cell}}m_{\text{ion}}c_{s}}(m_{\chi}v)^{3}&(\text{acoustic, $m_{\chi}v\lesssim a^{-1}$})\,,\\ \frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}^{2}}{m_{\text{cell}}m_{\text{ion}}\langle\omega\rangle}(m_{\chi}v)^{4}&(\text{otherwise})\,,\end{cases}
Rmagnon\displaystyle R_{\text{magnon}} ∼\displaystyle\sim ρχmχ​1mcell​gχ2​ge2mV4​Sion​∫d​q​q∼gχ2​ge2mV4​ρχmχ​Sionmcell​(mχ​v)2.\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}}\,S_{\text{ion}}\int dq\,q\sim\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{V}^{4}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}}{m_{\text{cell}}}(m_{\chi}v)^{2}\,. (48)

Fixing RR, the coupling plotted in Fig. 1, gχ​ge​mχ2mV2g_{\chi}g_{e}\frac{m_{\chi}^{2}}{m_{V}^{2}} scales as mχm_{\chi}, mχ1/2m_{\chi}^{1/2} and mχ3/2m_{\chi}^{3/2}, respectively, in the three cases, in agreement with the high-mχm_{\chi} behaviors of the dashed blue, solid blue and red curves in Fig. 1, respectively. Also, magnons have better sensitivity than phonons to the SD coupling by a factor of RmagnonRphonon∼mion​ω/Sionmχ​v\sqrt{\frac{R_{\text{magnon}}}{R_{\text{phonon}}}}\sim\frac{\sqrt{m_{\text{ion}}\omega/S_{\text{ion}}}}{m_{\chi}v}, and the advantage becomes more significant at smaller mχm_{\chi} (though the magnon curve hits the kinematic threshold at higher mχm_{\chi} due to the dispersion being quadratic).

III.2 Scalar Mediator Models

We next consider scalar mediator models with both scalar and pseudoscalar couplings. We take the mediator couplings to SM fermions to be proportional to their masses, gψ∝mψg_{\psi}\propto m_{\psi} (motivated by Higgs-portal hidden sector theories, see Ref. [98] for a recent review), and consider each of the four combinations of currents, which we denote by S×SS\times S, P×SP\times S, S×PS\times P and P×PP\times P. Among them, S×SS\times S (i.e. standard SI considered previously in Refs. [53, 54, 33, 34]) and P×SP\times S can excite phonons via the N{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N} response,99 9 These models generate additional operators when matched onto the NR EFT beyond leading order, which could excite magnons. We do not consider magnon excitation here due to the severely suppressed rate. The same applies to the SI and electric dipole DM models in Sec. III.3. while S×PS\times P and P×PP\times P can excite both phonons and magnons in a magnetically ordered target via the S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S} response. However, similar to the standard SD interaction in Sec. III.1, the phonon excitation rate will be suppressed relative to the magnon excitation rate, so we focus on the latter here. We obtain the following expressions for the differential rates defined in Eq. (41):

Σν​(𝒒)phononS×S\displaystyle\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})_{\text{phonon}}^{S\times S} =\displaystyle= gχ2(q2+mϕ2)2​|∑ψgψeff​FN,ν(ψ)|2,\displaystyle\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}}{(q^{2}+m_{\phi}^{2})^{2}}\,\Bigl|\sum_{\psi}g_{\psi}^{\text{eff}}F_{N,\nu}^{(\psi)}\Bigr|^{2}\,, (49)
Σν​(𝒒)phononP×S\displaystyle\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})_{\text{phonon}}^{P\times S} =\displaystyle= gχ2(q2+mϕ2)2​q24​mχ2​|∑ψgψeff​FN,ν(ψ)|2,\displaystyle\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}}{(q^{2}+m_{\phi}^{2})^{2}}\frac{q^{2}}{4m_{\chi}^{2}}\,\Bigl|\sum_{\psi}g_{\psi}^{\text{eff}}F_{N,\nu}^{(\psi)}\Bigr|^{2}\,, (50)
Σν​(𝒒)magnonS×P\displaystyle\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})_{\text{magnon}}^{S\times P} =\displaystyle= gχ2​ge2(q2+mϕ2)2​q2me2​|𝒒^⋅𝑬S,ν|2,\displaystyle\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{(q^{2}+m_{\phi}^{2})^{2}}\frac{q^{2}}{m_{e}^{2}}\,\Bigl|\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\cdot\boldsymbol{E}_{S,\nu}\Bigr|^{2}\,, (51)
Σν​(𝒒)magnonP×P\displaystyle\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})_{\text{magnon}}^{P\times P} =\displaystyle= gχ2​ge2(q2+mϕ2)2​q44​mχ2​me2​|𝒒^⋅𝑬S,ν|2.\displaystyle\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{(q^{2}+m_{\phi}^{2})^{2}}\frac{q^{4}}{4m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}\,\Bigl|\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\cdot\boldsymbol{E}_{S,\nu}\Bigr|^{2}\,. (52)

Note that for the S×SS\times S and P×SP\times S models, screening effects have been taken into account by using gψeffg_{\psi}^{\text{eff}} in place of gψg_{\psi}, as discussed around Eq. (14); the dielectric tensors 𝛆∞\boldsymbol{\upvarepsilon}_{\infty} of the phonon targets GaAs and SiO2 are obtained from DFT calculations [56].

In Fig. 2, we plot the expected rate for each of the four coupling combinations, for a common value for the product of couplings, to illustrate the hierarchy between the rate from the different interactions. We have chosen to show the rate instead of projected reach here so that the general case where more than one types of interactions are present, it would be straightforward to rescale the curves to see which one is dominant. For example, if gχ(S)∼gχ(P)g_{\chi}^{(S)}\sim g_{\chi}^{(P)}, gψ(S)∼gψ(P)g_{\psi}^{(S)}\sim g_{\psi}^{(P)}, we have the highest rate from phonon excitations via the S×SS\times S coupling, i.e. the standard SI interaction, as expected. On the other hand, if the couplings to SM fermions are dominantly pseudoscalar, gψ(P)/gψ(S)≳107g_{\psi}^{(P)}/g_{\psi}^{(S)}\gtrsim 10^{7}, magnon excitations have better sensitivity than phonon excitations for the same exposure; this is one of the benchmark models considered previously in Ref. [57]. The hierarchy seen in Fig. 2, and also some main features of the curves, can be understood following Eqs. (43) and (44), as we now explain.

First consider the light mediator case, mV≪qm_{V}\ll q (left panel of Fig. 2). For phonon excitations in the S×SS\times S and P×SP\times S models, since the couplings to all ions have the same sign, the rate is dominated by acoustic phonons. For qq within the 1BZ, setting ω∼cs​q\omega\sim c_{s}q, we obtain

RphononS×S\displaystyle R_{\text{phonon}}^{S\times S} ∼\displaystyle\sim ρχmχ​1mcell​gχ2​gp2​⟨Np,n⟩2mion​∫d​q​1q​ω∼gχ2​gp2​ρχmχ​⟨Np,n⟩2mcell​mion​1ωmin,\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\,g_{\chi}^{2}g_{p}^{2}\,\frac{\langle N_{p,n}\rangle^{2}}{m_{\text{ion}}}\int dq\,\frac{1}{q\omega}\sim g_{\chi}^{2}g_{p}^{2}\,\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\langle N_{p,n}\rangle^{2}}{m_{\text{cell}}m_{\text{ion}}}\frac{1}{\omega_{\text{min}}}\,, (53)

where ωmin=cs​qmin\omega_{\text{min}}=c_{s}q_{\text{min}}. These are consistent with the mχ−1m_{\chi}^{-1} and mχ−2m_{\chi}^{-2} scaling of the green and purple curves for mχm_{\chi} up to ∼\sim MeV. Also, consistent with the figure, the ratio between them is RphononP×SRphononS×S∼ωminmχ​vcs∼10−6​ωmin1​meV​10−1​MeVmχ​v10−3​10−5cs\frac{R_{\text{phonon}}^{P\times S}}{R_{\text{phonon}}^{S\times S}}\sim\frac{\omega_{\text{min}}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{v}{c_{s}}\sim 10^{-6}\,\frac{\omega_{\text{min}}}{1\,\text{meV}}\frac{10^{-1}\,\text{MeV}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{v}{10^{-3}}\frac{10^{-5}}{c_{s}} for couplings of the same size. For heavier DM, on the other hand, momentum transfers beyond the 1BZ are allowed. For the S×SS\times S model, this is irrelevant since the integral is dominated by small qq, so the mχ−1m_{\chi}^{-1} trend continues past MeV. For the P×SP\times S model, since the integral is dominated by high qq where ω\omega no longer scales with qq, we have v2⟨ω⟩\frac{v^{2}}{\langle\omega\rangle} in place of vmχ​cs\frac{v}{m_{\chi}c_{s}} in Eq. (54). This explains the mχ−1m_{\chi}^{-1} scaling of the purple curves past mχ∼m_{\chi}\sim MeV in the left panel of Fig. 2.

For magnon excitations in the S×PS\times P and P×PP\times P models, we have

RmagnonS×P\displaystyle R_{\text{magnon}}^{S\times P} ∼\displaystyle\sim ρχmχ​1mcell​gχ2​ge2​Sionme2​∫d​q​1q∼gχ2​ge2​ρχmχ​Sionmcell​me2,\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}}{m_{e}^{2}}\int dq\,\frac{1}{q}\sim g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}\,\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}}{m_{\text{cell}}m_{e}^{2}}\,, (55)

again consistent with the mχ−1m_{\chi}^{-1} scaling of the corresponding curves in Fig. 2 (though the YIG curves have a bump near MeV due to the gapped magnons starting to contribute, as discussed in Ref. [57], which slightly obscures the overall scaling with mχm_{\chi}). This is consistent with what we see in Fig. 2.

The heavy mediator case, mV≫qm_{V}\gg q (right panel of Fig. 2), follows a similar analysis. All the qq integrals are now peaked at qmax∼mχ​vq_{\text{max}}\sim m_{\chi}v, and we find

These equations explain both the hierarchy of the rates for the four models, and the mχm_{\chi} scaling: in all cases, R​mV4mχ4∼mχ−1R\,\frac{m_{V}^{4}}{m_{\chi}^{4}}\sim m_{\chi}^{-1} at large mχm_{\chi}, while the phonon curves switch to mχ−2m_{\chi}^{-2} scaling below ∼\sim MeV.

III.3 Multipole Dark Matter Models

We now turn to the electric dipole, magnetic dipole, and anapole DM models in Table 2. For comparison, we also include the SI interaction model with a vector mediator. Motivated by the kinetic mixing benchmark, we assume the mediator couples to electric charge, gp=−geg_{p}=-g_{e}, gn=0g_{n}=0, and is much lighter than the smallest momentum transfer, mV≪m_{V}\ll eV. The SI and electric dipole DM models generate 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪11\mathcal{O}_{11} at leading order, respectively, both of which induce only the N{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N} response, which can be probed by single phonon excitation. The differential rates are

(62)

Eq. (61) is in agreement with previous results in Refs. [54, 33, 34]. A comparison of the phonon reach in these models is shown in the left panel of Fig. 3. The center and right panels of Fig. 3 zoom in on the magnetic dipole and anapole DM models, respectively, and compare the reach of phonon and magnon excitations.

We can carry out a similar analysis as in the previous subsections to understand the main features in Fig. 3. For single phonon excitation in GaAs and SiO2, we keep only the FN,ν(ψ)F_{N,\nu}^{(\psi)} terms in the Σν​(𝒒)\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q}) formulae above, and note that, as in the SI case discussed previously in Refs. [53, 54, 33, 34], the DM-ion couplings, being proportional to ⟨Np⟩−⟨Ne⟩=Qion\langle N_{p}\rangle-\langle N_{e}\rangle=Q_{\text{ion}}, have opposite signs for oppositely charged ions, so the optical phonon modes with ω∼q0\omega\sim q^{0} give the dominant contributions. Using Eqs. (43) and (44), we obtain the following parametric estimates:

RphononSI\displaystyle R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{SI}} ∼\displaystyle\sim ρχmχ​1mcell​gχ2​ge2ε∞2​Qion2mion​ω​∫d​q​1q∼gχ2​ge2​ρχmχ​(Qion2ε∞2​mcell​mion​ω),\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{\varepsilon_{\infty}^{2}}\frac{Q_{\text{ion}}^{2}}{m_{\text{ion}}\omega}\int dq\,\frac{1}{q}\sim g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}\,\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\biggl(\frac{Q_{\text{ion}}^{2}}{\varepsilon_{\infty}^{2}m_{\text{cell}}m_{\text{ion}}\omega}\biggr)\,, (67)
RphononedmRphononSI\displaystyle\frac{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{edm}}}{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{SI}}} ∼\displaystyle\sim RphononmdmRphononedm∼RphononanaRphononmdm∼v2,\displaystyle\frac{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{mdm}}}{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{edm}}}\sim\frac{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{ana}}}{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{mdm}}}\sim v^{2}\,, (68)
Rmagnonmdm\displaystyle R_{\text{magnon}}^{\text{mdm}} ∼\displaystyle\sim ρχmχ​Sionmcell​gχ2​ge2mχ2​me2​∫d​q​q∼gχ2​ge2​ρχmχ​Sion​v2mcell​me2,\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}}{m_{\text{cell}}}\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}\int dq\,q\sim g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}\,\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{S_{\text{ion}}v^{2}}{m_{\text{cell}}m_{e}^{2}}\,, (69)
RmagnonanaRmagnonmdm\displaystyle\frac{R_{\text{magnon}}^{\text{ana}}}{R_{\text{magnon}}^{\text{mdm}}} ∼\displaystyle\sim v2.\displaystyle v^{2}\,. (70)

Several comments are in order. First, Eq. (68) explains the hierarchy of sensitivity of phonon excitations to the four models in the left panel of Fig. 3, while Eq. (70) shows a similar hierarchy of sensitivity of magnon excitations to the magnetic dipole and anapole DM models. Also, note that in all cases, R∼mχ−1R\sim m_{\chi}^{-1}, so the reach on gχ​geg_{\chi}g_{e} scales as mχ1/2m_{\chi}^{1/2}, as seen in Fig. 3.

Next, let us compare the reach of different target materials, and via phonons versus magnons. For phonon excitations, the factor in parentheses in Eq. (67) reproduces the “quality factor” identified in Ref. [34], up to 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) factors we have dropped here. It captures the material properties that determine the sensitivity to the SI model with a dark photon mediator, and is the quantity to maximize in order to optimize target choice. For example, SiO2 has a quality factor that is about 80 times that of GaAs, which explains its significantly better reach, by almost an order of magnitude on the coupling gχ​geg_{\chi}g_{e}, as seen in Fig. 3 (and also previously in Ref. [34]).

For magnon excitations for the magnetic dipole and anapole DM models, we have considered YIG, which probes only the S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S} response, and α\alpha-RuCl3, which probes both S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S} and L{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L}. Since for these models, DM couples to the linear combination 2​𝑺e+𝑳e2\boldsymbol{S}_{e}+\boldsymbol{L}_{e} – the spin of an elementary particle has a Landé gg-factor of 2 – the additional L{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L} response that α\alpha-RuCl3 has does not qualitatively improve the sensitivity. Indeed, we see from Fig. 3 that YIG and α\alpha-RuCl3 have very similar reach around mχ∼0.1m_{\chi}\sim 0.1\,MeV. At higher mχm_{\chi}, YIG performs better due to additional contributions from the large number of gapped magnon modes. On the other hand, α\alpha-RuCl3 extends the reach down to much lower mχ∼m_{\chi}\sim keV. As discussed previously, this is because the magnon modes at zero momentum are gapped at a few meV (in contrast to YIG which has a gapless magnon branch that dominates the coupling to DM in the low momentum transfer limit).

Finally, we can compare the magnon and phonon excitation rates for the two models (magnetic dipole and anapole DM) where both are available. Let us denote 𝒬≡Qion2ε∞2​mp2mcell​mion​1​meVω{\cal Q}\equiv\frac{Q_{\text{ion}}^{2}}{\varepsilon_{\infty}^{2}}\frac{m_{p}^{2}}{m_{\text{cell}}m_{\text{ion}}}\frac{1\,\text{meV}}{\omega}, which is the phonon quality factor with the dimensionful parameters normalized in a way close to Ref. [34]. Its values are typically 𝒪⁡(10−7CLOSE\mathcal{O}(10^{-7}-OPEN10−5)10^{-5}), with GaAs and SiO2 residing on the lower and higher ends of the interval, respectively. We find

RphononmdmRmagnonmdm∼RphononanaRmagnonana∼𝒬​mcell​me2​v2Sion​mp2⋅1​meV∼10−4​(𝒬1.4×10−7),\frac{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{mdm}}}{R_{\text{magnon}}^{\text{mdm}}}\sim\frac{R_{\text{phonon}}^{\text{ana}}}{R_{\text{magnon}}^{\text{ana}}}\sim\frac{{\cal Q}\,m_{\text{cell}}m_{e}^{2}v^{2}}{S_{\text{ion}}m_{p}^{2}\cdot 1\,\text{meV}}\sim 10^{-4}\,\biggl(\frac{{\cal Q}}{1.4\times 10^{-7}}\biggr)\,, (71)

where mcellm_{\text{cell}} is for the target for magnon excitations, and we have substituted the numbers for YIG in the last equation. We see that, for the magnetic dipole and anapole DM models, magnons are indeed more sensitive than phonons, though choosing high phonon quality factor targets, such as SiO2 with 𝒬∼10−5{\cal Q}\sim 10^{-5} can approach the magnon sensitivity. Up to 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) factors, this is consistent with the center and right panels of Fig. 3.

III.4 (𝑳⋅𝑺)(\boldsymbol{L}\cdot\boldsymbol{S})-Interacting Dark Matter

We finally consider the (𝑳⋅𝑺)(\boldsymbol{L}\cdot\boldsymbol{S})-interacting DM model, which induces N{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N}, S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S} and L⊗S{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L\otimes S} responses. Taking the mediator to couple only to electrons for simplicity, we obtain the differential rates:

Σν​(𝒒)phonon\displaystyle\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q})_{\text{phonon}} =\displaystyle= gχ2​ge2(q2+mV2)2{|q24​me2[(1+κ)FN,ν(e)+2tr((𝟙−𝒒^𝒒^)⋅𝐅L⊗S,ν(e))]+(i​𝒒me×𝒗)⋅𝑭S,ν(e)|2\displaystyle\frac{g_{\chi}^{2}g_{e}^{2}}{(q^{2}+m_{V}^{2})^{2}}\biggl\{\,\biggl|\frac{q^{2}}{4m_{e}^{2}}\Bigl[(1+\kappa)F_{N,\nu}^{(e)}+2\,\text{tr}\bigl((\mathbb{1}-\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\boldsymbol{\hat{q}})\cdot{\bf F}_{L\otimes S,\nu}^{(e)}\bigr)\Bigr]+\biggl(\frac{i\boldsymbol{q}}{m_{e}}\times\boldsymbol{v}\biggr)\cdot\boldsymbol{F}_{S,\nu}^{(e)}\biggr|^{2} (72)
+q44​mχ2​me2|(𝟙−𝒒^𝒒^)⋅𝑭S,ν(e)|2},\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\;+\frac{q^{4}}{4m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}\Bigl|(\mathbb{1}-\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\boldsymbol{\hat{q}})\cdot\boldsymbol{F}_{S,\nu}^{(e)}\Bigr|^{2}\biggr\}\,,

(73)

In the absence of magnetic order, 𝑭S,ν(e)=0\boldsymbol{F}_{S,\nu}^{(e)}=0. Also, unless κ\kappa is tuned to be very close to −1-1, we do not expect the 𝐅L⊗S,ν(e){\bf F}_{L\otimes S,\nu}^{(e)} term in Eq. (72) to dominate — the total spin-orbit coupling vanishes for full shells, and is otherwise often suppressed by crystal fields, especially for lighter elements. Thus, while an interesting feature of this model, the coupling to 𝑳⋅𝑺\boldsymbol{L}\cdot\boldsymbol{S} does not suggest a better probe than searching for phonon excitations via the N{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N} response with already proposed target materials. In Fig. 4, we include only the FN,ν(e)F_{N,\nu}^{(e)} term when computing phonon reach for GaAs and SiO2, and for concreteness set κ=0\kappa=0. Since the total electron numbers of ions are all positive, the rate is dominated by acoustic phonons, with ω∼cs​q\omega\sim c_{s}q. Again using Eqs. (43) and (44), we can estimate

The magnon reach curves for YIG and α\alpha-RuCl3 can be understood in a similar way. We have

So the magnon reach becomes better at lower mχm_{\chi}, as we can see in Fig. 4. IV Conclusions

We have formulated an EFT framework for computing direct detection rates via single phonon and magnon excitations for general DM interactions, and illustrated its application with a set of benchmark models, listed in Table 2, that cover a wide range of possibilities for a spin-12\frac{1}{2} DM particle interacting with SM fermions ψ=p,n,e\psi=p,n,e (proton, neutron and electron). The procedure consists of first matching a relativistic DM model onto a set of NR effective operators, listed in Table 3, and then matching these operators onto lattice degrees of freedom, including particle numbers ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle}, spins ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}, orbital angular momenta ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle} and spin-orbit couplings ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\bigl\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\bigr\rangle} for the ψ=p,n,e\psi=p,n,e particles in an ion. These define the four types of crystal responses and enter the rate formula for single phonon excitation, while a subset of them – ⟨𝑺e⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{e}\rangle} and ⟨𝑳e⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{e}\rangle} – also enter the rate formula for single magnon excitation.

A practical prescription for computing direct detection rates, as explained around Eq. (41), utilizes the central formula, Eq. (), which gives the lattice scattering potential in terms of the effective operator coefficients ci(ψ)c_{i}^{(\psi)}. Upon plugging in the ci(ψ)c_{i}^{(\psi)}’s generated by a relativistic theory of DM (listed in Table 2 for our benchmark models), one simply replaces the ionic expectation values ⟨Xψ⟩l​j{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle X_{\psi}\rangle}_{lj} by FX,ν(ψ)F_{X,\nu}^{(\psi)} defined in Eq. (39) (for ψ=p,n,e\psi=p,n,e and X=N,S,L,L⊗SX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}N},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L\otimes S}) or 𝑬X,ν\boldsymbol{E}_{X,\nu} defined in Eq. (40) (for ψ=e\psi=e and X=S,LX={\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}S},{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}L}), squares the expression and takes the DM spin average. This gives the differential rates Σν​(𝒒)\Sigma_{\nu}(\boldsymbol{q}), which are then substituted into Eqs. (41) and (42) for the total rate of single phonon or magnon excitation.

The set of crystal responses that we have identified point to various possibilities of optimizing detector target choice. However, a general observation from our calculations in Sec. III is that, among the four types of crystal responses, ⟨Nψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle N_{\psi}\rangle} and ⟨𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\rangle}, which are associated with point-like degrees of freedom, tend to dominate the rate, compared to the composite responses ⟨𝑳ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\rangle} and ⟨𝑳ψ⊗𝑺ψ⟩{\color[rgb]{0.72,0,0}\bigl\langle\boldsymbol{L}_{\psi}\otimes\boldsymbol{S}_{\psi}\bigr\rangle}. This implies that, purely from the point of view of maximizing the rate, exotic materials with orbital orders or strong spin-orbit couplings are not necessary for improving the reach to a broad class of DM models.

Meanwhile, as phonon DM experiments focused on crystal targets, such as SPICE (Sub-eV Polar Interactions Cryogenic Experiment), which is part of the TESSERACT (Transition Edge Sensors with Sub-EV Resolution And Cryogenic Targets) project [88], move into R&D, it is important to note that their discovery potential extends well beyond the simplest models with spin-independent interactions studied previously. As we showed in Sec. III, phonon excitations have broad sensitivity to light DM models. Perhaps surprisingly, with judicious choice of target material, phonon excitations may even be competitive with magnon excitations for some DM models where the latter is expected to have a parametrically higher rate, such as the magnetic dipole and anapole DM models. Given the greater challenges associated with single magnon detection relative to phonons, this is encouraging for phonon-based experiments in the near term.

Appendix A Nonrelativistic Matching for a Fermion Field

In this appendix, we review the procedure of decomposing a Dirac fermion field ψ\psi in the NR limit. Consider the following unperturbed relativistic Lagrangian:

ℒ0=ψ¯i(∂μ−iAμ)γμψ−mψψ¯ψ.\mathcal{L}_{0}=\bar{\psi}\,i(\partial_{\mu}-iA_{\mu})\gamma^{\mu}\psi-m_{\psi}\bar{\psi}\psi\,. (78)

In free space, we would expand the ψ\psi field in plane waves multiplied by the usual uu, vv spinors satisfying the free particle Dirac equation. Here, we allow the presence of an external gauge potential Aμ=(Φ,𝑨)A^{\mu}=(\Phi,\boldsymbol{A}), which may not be a small perturbation. For example, if ψ\psi is an electron in a crystal, it is bound by the electromagnetic potential from the ions, and the bound state wavefunctions are very different from plane waves. Generally, we can expand the ψ\psi field in the basis of energy eigenstate wavefunctions. Dropping the antiparticle part, we have

ψ⁡(𝒙,t)=∑IuI​(𝒙,t)​b^I=∑Ie−i​EI​t​uI​(𝒙)​b^I,\psi(\boldsymbol{x},t)=\sum_{I}u_{I}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\,\hat{b}_{I}=\sum_{I}e^{-iE_{I}t}\,u_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})\,\hat{b}_{I}\,, (79)

where the cc-number uIu_{I} spinors satisfy

(EIγ0−i𝜸⋅∇−mψ−γ0Φ(𝒙)+𝜸⋅𝑨(𝒙))uI(𝒙)=0.\bigl(E_{I}\gamma^{0}-i\boldsymbol{\gamma}\cdot\nabla-m_{\psi}-\gamma^{0}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})+\boldsymbol{\gamma}\cdot\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x})\bigr)\,u_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})=0\,. (80)

Writing

uI​(𝒙)=12​(ΨI​(𝒙)+ΘI​(𝒙)ΨI​(𝒙)−ΘI​(𝒙)),u_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{matrix}\Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})+\Theta_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})\\ \Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})-\Theta_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})\end{matrix}\right)\,, (81)

with ΨI\Psi_{I}, ΘI\Theta_{I} two-component wavefunctions, we see that Eq. (80) is solved by

ΘI​(𝒙)=i​𝝈⋅(∇−i​𝑨​(𝒙))EI+mψ−Φ⁡(𝒙)​ΨI​(𝒙).\Theta_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})=\frac{i\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\bigl(\nabla-i\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x})\bigr)}{E_{I}+m_{\psi}-\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})}\,\Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})\,. (82)

This immediately leads to Eq. (8), repeated here for easy reference:

ψ⁡(𝒙,t)=e−i​mψ​t​12​((1−𝝈⋅𝒌2​mψ+ε)​ψ+​(𝒙,t)(1+𝝈⋅𝒌2​mψ+ε)​ψ+​(𝒙,t)),\psi(\boldsymbol{x},t)=e^{-im_{\psi}t}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{matrix}\Bigl(1-\frac{\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{k}}{2m_{\psi}+\varepsilon}\Bigr)\,\psi^{+}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\\ \Bigl(1+\frac{\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{k}}{2m_{\psi}+\varepsilon}\Bigr)\,\psi^{+}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\end{matrix}\right), (83)

where 𝒌=−i∇−𝑨\boldsymbol{k}=-i\nabla-\boldsymbol{A}, ε=i∂t−Φ\varepsilon=i\partial_{t}-\Phi, and ψ+​(𝒙,t)=∑Ie−i​εI​t​ΨI​(𝒙)​b^I\psi^{+}(\boldsymbol{x},t)=\sum_{I}e^{-i\varepsilon_{I}t}\,\Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})\,\hat{b}_{I} with εI=EI−mψ\varepsilon_{I}=E_{I}-m_{\psi}. The prefactor has been chosen such that the NR field ψ±\psi^{\pm}’s kinetic term is normalized at leading order as in Eq. (11).

In the NR limit, |ΘI|≪|ΦI||\Theta_{I}|\ll|\Phi_{I}|. The large component ΨI\Psi_{I} satisfies

[−𝝈⋅(∇−i𝑨(𝒙))12​mψ+εI−Φ⁡(𝒙)𝝈⋅(∇−i𝑨(𝒙))+Φ(𝒙)]ΨI(𝒙)=εIΨI(𝒙).\biggl[-\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\bigl(\nabla-i\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x})\bigr)\,\frac{1}{2m_{\psi}+\varepsilon_{I}-\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\bigl(\nabla-i\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x})\bigr)+\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})\biggr]\Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})=\varepsilon_{I}\Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})\,. (84)

At leading order, we replace 12​mψ+εI−Φ⁡(𝒙)→12​mψ\frac{1}{2m_{\psi}+\varepsilon_{I}-\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})}\to\frac{1}{2m_{\psi}}, and recover the NR Schrödinger equation:

[−(∇−i​𝑨​(𝒙))22​mψ+12​mψ​𝝈⋅(∇×𝑨⁡(𝒙))+Φ⁡(𝒙)]​ΨI​(𝒙)=εI​ΨI​(𝒙).\biggl[-\frac{\bigl(\nabla-i\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x})\bigr)^{2}}{2m_{\psi}}+\frac{1}{2m_{\psi}}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\bigl(\nabla\times\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x})\bigr)+\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})\biggr]\Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})=\varepsilon_{I}\Psi_{I}(\boldsymbol{x})\,. (85)

Corrections to this equation can be incorporated order by order if needed.

Appendix B Projection of Angular Momentum Operators

In this appendix, we detail the steps that lead to the numbers λS,j=−13\lambda_{S,j}=-\frac{1}{3}, λL,j=−43\lambda_{L,j}=-\frac{4}{3} in the case of α\alpha-RuCl3, following the projection of angular momentum operators 𝑺e\boldsymbol{S}_{e}, 𝑳e\boldsymbol{L}_{e} in Eq. (32). The formation of effective ionic spins Sj=12S_{j}=\frac{1}{2} is due to the combined effect of crystal fields and spin-orbit coupling [82]. First, octahedral crystal fields split the five degenerate 3dd orbitals (ℓ=2\ell=2) of Ru3+ into two higher-energy ege_{g} orbitals and three lower-energy t2​gt_{2g} orbitals with an effective orbital moment ℓeff=1\ell_{\text{eff}}=1. The energy difference between the ege_{g} and t2​gt_{2g} orbitals is 𝒪⁡(eV)\mathcal{O}(\text{eV}), rendering the (unoccupied) ege_{g} orbitals irrelevant for the discussion. For the t2​gt_{2g} orbitals, spin-orbit coupling further splits these ℓeff=1\ell_{\text{eff}}=1 states into jeff=32j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{3}{2} and 12\frac{1}{2}. With five 3dd electrons, the lower-energy jeff=32j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{3}{2} states are fully occupied, while the higher-energy jeff=12j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2} Kramers doublet is occupied by a single electron — it is this electron that contributes to the magnetic order. Therefore, the goal is to project the angular momentum operators 𝑺\boldsymbol{S}, 𝑳\boldsymbol{L} (dropping subscript ee from here on for simplicity) onto the jeff=12j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2} subspace.

The first step is to project 𝑳\boldsymbol{L} onto the t2​gt_{2g} subspace. The t2​gt_{2g} states are denoted by dy​zd_{yz}, dz​xd_{zx}, dx​yd_{xy}. The angular part of their wavefunctions are linear combinations of spherical harmonics Yℓ=2m​(θ,ϕ)Y_{\ell=2}^{m}(\theta,\phi) (see e.g. Ref. [99]); equivalently, these t2​gt_{2g} states are linear combinations of |ℓ,mℓ⟩|\ell,m_{\ell}\rangle states with ℓ=2\ell=2:

|dy​z⟩=i2(|2,1⟩+|2,−1⟩),|dz​x⟩=−12(|2,1⟩−|2,−1⟩),|dx​y⟩=−i2(|2,2⟩−|2,−2⟩).|d_{yz}\rangle=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|2,1\rangle+|2,-1\rangle\bigr)\,,\quad|d_{zx}\rangle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|2,1\rangle-|2,-1\rangle\bigr)\,,\quad|d_{xy}\rangle=-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|2,2\rangle-|2,-2\rangle\bigr)\,. (86)

To compute 𝒫t2​g​𝑳​𝒫t2​g\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}\boldsymbol{L}\,\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}, with the projection operator

𝒫t2​g=|dy​z⟩​⟨dy​z|+|dz​x⟩​⟨dz​x|+|dx​y⟩​⟨dx​y|,\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}=|d_{yz}\rangle\langle d_{yz}|+|d_{zx}\rangle\langle d_{zx}|+|d_{xy}\rangle\langle d_{xy}|\,, (87)

we make use of the familiar formulae

⟨ℓ′,mℓ′​|Lz|​ℓ,mℓ⟩=mℓ​δℓ′,ℓ​δmℓ′,mℓ,⟨ℓ′,mℓ′​|L±|​ℓ,mℓ⟩=(ℓ∓mℓ)​(ℓ±mℓ+1)​δℓ′,ℓ​δmℓ′,mℓ±1,\langle\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}_{\ell}|L_{z}|\ell,m_{\ell}\rangle=m_{\ell}\,\delta_{\ell^{\prime},\ell}\delta_{m^{\prime}_{\ell},m_{\ell}}\,,\qquad\langle\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}_{\ell}|L_{\pm}|\ell,m_{\ell}\rangle=\sqrt{(\ell\mp m_{\ell})(\ell\pm m_{\ell}+1)}\,\delta_{\ell^{\prime},\ell}\delta_{m^{\prime}_{\ell},m_{\ell}\pm 1}\,, (88)

where L±=Lx±i​LyL_{\pm}=L_{x}\pm iL_{y}, and obtain, for the matrix representation in the |dy​z⟩|d_{yz}\rangle, |dz​x⟩|d_{zx}\rangle, |dx​y⟩|d_{xy}\rangle basis:

𝒫t2​g​Lz​𝒫t2​g​=˙​(0i  0−i 0  00 0  0),𝒫t2​g​L±​𝒫t2​g​=˙​(0 0±10 0i∓1−i  0).\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}\,L_{z}\,\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}\;\dot{=}\;\begin{pmatrix}0&\;i\;&\;\;0\;\;\\ -i&\;0\;&\;\;0\;\;\\ 0&\;0\;&\;\;0\;\;\end{pmatrix}\,,\qquad\quad\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}\,L_{\pm}\,\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}\;\dot{=}\;\begin{pmatrix}0&\;0\;&\pm 1\\ 0&\;0\;&\;\;i\;\;\\ \mp 1&-i&\;\;0\;\;\end{pmatrix}\,. (89)

These might not look familiar, but they are nothing but ℓ=1\ell=1 angular momentum operators in the |px⟩|p_{x}\rangle, |py⟩|p_{y}\rangle, |pz⟩|p_{z}\rangle basis, which is related to the |ℓ,mℓ⟩|\ell,m_{\ell}\rangle basis with ℓ=1\ell=1 by [99]

|px⟩=−12(|1,1⟩−|1,−1⟩),|py⟩=i2(|1,1⟩+|1,−1⟩),|pz⟩=|1,0⟩.|p_{x}\rangle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|1,1\rangle-|1,-1\rangle\bigr)\,,\qquad|p_{y}\rangle=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|1,1\rangle+|1,-1\rangle\bigr)\,,\qquad|p_{z}\rangle=|1,0\rangle\,. (90)

The angular momentum operators in this basis read

Lz​=˙​(  0−i 0i0 0  00 0),L±​=˙​(0 0∓10 0−i±1i  0).L_{z}\;\dot{=}\;\begin{pmatrix}\;\;0\;\;&-i&\;0\;\;\\ \;\;i\;\;&0&\;0\;\;\\ \;\;0\;\;&0&\;0\;\;\end{pmatrix}\,,\qquad\quad L_{\pm}\;\dot{=}\;\begin{pmatrix}0&\;0\;&\mp 1\\ 0&\;0\;&\;\;-i\;\;\\ \pm 1&\;i\;&\;\;0\;\;\end{pmatrix}\,. (91)

Comparing Eq. (89) and (91), we see that 𝑳\boldsymbol{L} acts as an effective angular momentum with ℓ=1\ell=1 on the t2​gt_{2g} subspace:

𝒫t2​g​𝑳​𝒫t2​g=−𝑳eff(ℓ=1).\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}\,\boldsymbol{L}\,\mathcal{P}_{t_{2g}}=-\boldsymbol{L}_{\text{eff}}^{(\ell=1)}\,. (92)

The second step is to combine this effective orbital angular momentum ℓeff=1\ell_{\text{eff}}=1 with the electron’s spin s=12s=\frac{1}{2}. This follows the standard angular momentum addition, and we obtain, for the jeff=12j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2} states:

|jeff=12,mjeff=12⟩\displaystyle\bigl|j_{\text{eff}}=\tfrac{1}{2},m_{j_{\text{eff}}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\rangle =\displaystyle= 23|mℓeff=1,ms=−12⟩−13|mℓeff=0,ms=12⟩,\displaystyle\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\,\bigl|m_{\ell_{\text{eff}}}=1,m_{s}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\rangle-\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\,\bigl|m_{\ell_{\text{eff}}}=0,m_{s}=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\rangle\,, (93)
|jeff=12,mjeff=−12⟩\displaystyle\bigl|j_{\text{eff}}=\tfrac{1}{2},m_{j_{\text{eff}}}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\rangle =\displaystyle= 13|mℓeff=0,ms=−12⟩−23|mℓeff=−1,ms=12⟩,\displaystyle\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\,\bigl|m_{\ell_{\text{eff}}}=0,m_{s}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\rangle-\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\,\bigl|m_{\ell_{\text{eff}}}=-1,m_{s}=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr\rangle\,, (94)

where the coefficients are Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. It is now straightforward to project 𝑳eff\boldsymbol{L}_{\text{eff}} and 𝑺\boldsymbol{S} onto the jeff=12j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2} subspace:

𝒫jeff=12​Lzeff​𝒫jeff=12​=˙​(230 0−23),𝒫jeff=12​L+eff​𝒫jeff=12​=˙​( 043 0  0),\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\,L_{z}^{\text{eff}}\,\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\dot{=}\begin{pmatrix}\;\frac{2}{3}\;\;&0\;\\ \;0\;\;&-\frac{2}{3}\;\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\,L_{+}^{\text{eff}}\,\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\dot{=}\begin{pmatrix}\;0\;&\;\;\frac{4}{3}\;\\ \;0\;&\;\;0\;\end{pmatrix}\,, (95)
𝒫jeff=12​Sz​𝒫jeff=12​=˙​(−16 0016),𝒫jeff=12​S+​𝒫jeff=12​=˙​( 0−13 00).\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\,S_{z}\,\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\dot{=}\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{1}{6}&\;0\;\\ 0&\;\frac{1}{6}\;\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\,S_{+}\,\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\dot{=}\begin{pmatrix}\;0\;\;&-\frac{1}{3}\;\\ \;0\;\;&0\;\end{pmatrix}\,. (96)

We see that both 𝑳eff\boldsymbol{L}_{\text{eff}} and 𝑺\boldsymbol{S} are proportional to 𝑱eff=𝝈2\boldsymbol{J}_{\text{eff}}=\frac{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}{2} (identified as the total ionic spin as discussed above) when acting on the jeff=12j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2} subspace. So finally, we obtain

𝒫jeff=12​𝑳​𝒫jeff=12=−𝒫jeff=12​𝑳eff​𝒫jeff=12=−43​𝑱eff,𝒫jeff=12​𝑺​𝒫jeff=12=−13​𝑱eff.\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\,\boldsymbol{L}\,\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}=-\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\,\boldsymbol{L}_{\text{eff}}\,\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}=-\frac{4}{3}\boldsymbol{J}_{\text{eff}}\,,\qquad\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}\,\boldsymbol{S}\,\mathcal{P}_{j_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}}=-\frac{1}{3}\boldsymbol{J}_{\text{eff}}\,. (97)

=\displaystyle= 4​π2N0​q∫0vescdvv3e−v2/v02∫−11dcosθδ(cosθ−v∗v)[cos2θ𝒒^𝒒^+12sin2θ(𝟙−𝒒^𝒒^)]\displaystyle\frac{4\pi^{2}}{N_{0}q}\int_{0}^{v_{\text{esc}}}dv\,v^{3}\,e^{-v^{2}/v_{0}^{2}}\int_{-1}^{1}d\cos\theta\,\delta\biggl(\cos\theta-\frac{v_{*}}{v}\biggr)\biggl[\cos^{2}\theta\,\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}+\frac{1}{2}\sin^{2}\theta(\mathbb{1}-\boldsymbol{\hat{q}}\boldsymbol{\hat{q}})\biggr]
